title: A reunion compares whole paths
question: Can reciprocal rate descriptions settle a reunion?
recap: Reunited clocks compare elapsed times along different paths between shared meetings. Flat-spacetime path accounting does not predict a real equator-versus-pole clock comparison by itself.
premises: Use ideal clocks following specified subluminal paths in flat spacetime.
The comparison fixes the departure and reunion events.
limitations: Real terrestrial comparisons also require gravitational effects.
Acceleration changes the path; no universal extra acceleration penalty is added to the clock formula.

overview.text: Reunited clocks compare elapsed times along different paths between shared meetings. Flat-spacetime path accounting does not predict a real equator-versus-pole clock comparison by itself.

full.spoken: An ideal clock’s elapsed proper time is the path integral of the square root of one minus its speed squared over c squared.

full.text: For two idealized inertial legs at speed magnitude 0.6c lasting a total of 10 coordinate seconds, the traveling clock accumulates 8 seconds when the turnaround duration is neglected. A clock remaining at rest accumulates 10. Each piece and its common endpoints must be specified.

The moving-clock laboratory distinguishes a transported-clock comparison from a statement about reciprocal rates between separated inertial clocks. The equator remark has a different boundary: a real rotating Earth includes gravity and is not decided by the flat-spacetime model alone.

full.returnCaption: Return to can reciprocal rate descriptions settle a reunion.

items: Specify each clock’s entire path between them.
Integrate the ideal elapsed-time law along each path.
For constant-speed legs, multiply each coordinate duration by the appropriate inverse γ.
Do not substitute a one-way visual delay for elapsed proper time.
Leave an Earth comparison outside the model when gravitational inputs are absent.

margin.text: The proper-time integral is modern explanatory notation. The source’s equator remark is preserved for the historical edition rather than silently “corrected”; the present laboratory explicitly refuses a special-relativity-only Earth prediction.
